title: Load Balancing, Proxies & CDN
summary: How load balancers distribute traffic, proxy types (forward/reverse), CDN architecture, and LB algorithms with internals.

explanation.overview: Load balancers distribute incoming traffic across multiple servers to ensure no single server becomes a bottleneck. They are the gateway to horizontal scaling — without a load balancer, you can't have multiple application servers. They also provide health checking, SSL termination, and failure isolation.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: A load balancer sits between clients and servers. The client connects to the LB's virtual IP (VIP). The LB selects a backend server using a configured algorithm, forwards the request, receives the response, and returns it to the client. The client never knows which backend server handled its request. Modern LBs operate at two layers: L4 (transport — routes based on IP/port, fast, no request inspection) and L7 (application — routes based on HTTP headers, URL path, cookies, slower but smarter).

children.title: Load Balancer Types & Layers
children.summary: L4 vs L7 load balancers and when to use each.

key_concepts.definition: Routes traffic based on IP address and TCP/UDP port. Does NOT inspect the request content (URL, headers, body). Simply forwards TCP connections. HOW IT WORKS: receives TCP SYN, selects backend using algorithm, rewrites destination IP (NAT) or establishes separate TCP connection (proxy mode). Extremely fast — operates at kernel level, handles millions of connections/sec. TOOLS: Linux IPVS (IP Virtual Server), AWS NLB (Network Load Balancer), HAProxy in TCP mode. USE WHEN: you need raw throughput and don't need content-based routing (database connections, gRPC, WebSocket, any non-HTTP protocol).

Routes traffic based on request content — URL path, HTTP method, headers, cookies, query parameters. Can make intelligent routing decisions: /api/* → API servers, /static/* → CDN origin, /admin/* → admin servers. HOW IT WORKS: terminates the client's TCP connection, reads the full HTTP request, applies routing rules, opens a new TCP connection to the selected backend, forwards the request. Terminates TLS here (SSL offloading — backends handle unencrypted traffic, reducing their CPU load). TOOLS: NGINX, HAProxy in HTTP mode, AWS ALB (Application Load Balancer), Envoy, Traefik. USE WHEN: HTTP-based services, content-based routing, A/B testing (route 10% to new version based on cookie), sticky sessions (route same user to same backend for session affinity).

Distributes traffic across multiple datacenters/regions. Typically DNS-based: health-checks all regions, returns IP of the healthiest/closest region. AWS Route 53 with latency-based routing, Cloudflare DNS load balancing. This is the first hop — then regional LBs distribute within each datacenter.

children.title: Load Balancing Algorithms
children.summary: How LBs choose which backend server to forward each request to.

key_concepts.definition: Distribute requests sequentially: server 1, server 2, server 3, server 1, ... SIMPLE but assumes all servers have equal capacity and all requests have equal cost. If one server is slower (hardware issue) or some requests are 100× more expensive (report generation vs health check), round robin creates imbalance. USE: stateless, homogeneous servers with uniform request cost.

Each server has a weight proportional to its capacity. Server A (weight 3): gets 3 requests per cycle. Server B (weight 1): gets 1 request per cycle. USE: heterogeneous hardware (some servers have more CPU/RAM). CONFIGURABLE: adjust weights based on observed capacity.

Route to the server with the fewest active connections. Naturally adapts to server speed — a fast server finishes connections quickly and receives more traffic. Better than round robin for variable request processing times. INTERNAL: LB maintains a counter per backend, incremented on new request, decremented when connection closes. Selection: pick the minimum. Complexity: O(N) scan or O(log N) with a min-heap.

hash(client_IP) % num_servers → always routes the same client to the same server. Provides implicit session affinity without cookies. PROBLEM: adding/removing a server changes the hash for all clients. FIX: use consistent hashing (see ch08) to minimize disruption.
Route to the server with the lowest average response time AND fewest active connections. Combines health awareness with load awareness. Most sophisticated algorithm — used by NGINX Plus and AWS ALB.

Randomly select a server. Statistically equivalent to round robin for large numbers of requests. Zero state tracking. Surprisingly effective at scale. VARIANT: Power of Two Random Choices — pick 2 random servers, send to the one with fewer connections. This achieves near-optimal load distribution with minimal overhead. Used by Envoy proxy.

advanced_tweaks.how: LB periodically pings each backend (HTTP GET /health every 10 seconds). If a server fails 3 consecutive checks, remove from pool. When it passes again, re-add. Types: TCP check (connection succeeds?), HTTP check (returns 200?), custom script. EDGE CASE: a server returns 200 on /health but is actually broken (database connection lost). FIX: deep health checks that verify downstream dependencies.

When removing a server (for deploy), stop sending NEW requests but allow existing connections to complete (drain period, typically 30-60 seconds). Prevents interrupted requests. AWS calls this 'deregistration delay'.

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: When backends don't need encrypted internal traffic
advanced_tweaks.how: LB terminates TLS, communicates with backends over HTTP. Reduces backend CPU (TLS is CPU-intensive, especially RSA). The LB handles certificate management. RE-ENCRYPTION: if internal traffic must be encrypted (zero trust), LB terminates client TLS, then re-encrypts with a separate internal cert (mTLS to backends).

children.title: Proxies — Forward & Reverse
children.summary: Forward proxies act on behalf of clients, reverse proxies act on behalf of servers.

key_concepts.definition: Sits between client and internet. Client → Forward Proxy → Internet. The proxy sends requests on behalf of the client. The destination server sees the proxy's IP, not the client's. USE CASES: corporate firewalls (block certain URLs), anonymity (VPN/Tor), caching (Squid proxy caches frequently accessed web pages for an office network). SYSTEM DESIGN: rarely discussed in interviews, but important to understand for security contexts.

Sits between internet and servers. Internet → Reverse Proxy → Backend Servers. The client sees the proxy's IP, not the backend's. Every load balancer is a reverse proxy. Additional capabilities: SSL termination, caching, compression, rate limiting, request routing, DDoS protection. TOOLS: NGINX (most popular), HAProxy, Envoy (Istio service mesh), Apache httpd. SYSTEM DESIGN: always draw a reverse proxy / LB / API Gateway between clients and your application servers.

A specialized reverse proxy for API management. Adds: authentication/authorization (validate JWT, API keys), rate limiting (per client, per endpoint), request/response transformation (add headers, rewrite URLs), aggregation (combine responses from multiple microservices into one response), monitoring (track per-endpoint latency, error rates). TOOLS: Kong, AWS API Gateway, Apigee, Tyk. In system design: always place an API Gateway in front of your microservices. It's the single entry point that handles cross-cutting concerns.

children.title: CDN — Content Delivery Network
children.summary: How CDNs distribute content globally via edge servers to minimize latency.

explanation.overview: A CDN is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers that cache content close to users. Instead of every request traveling to your origin server (potentially across continents), the nearest CDN PoP (Point of Presence) serves cached content. Reduces latency from ~200ms to ~20ms for global users.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: PULL CDN: On first request, PoP has no cache → forwards to origin → gets response → caches it locally → returns to client. Subsequent requests for the same content served from PoP cache (cache hit). Cache miss rate decreases as the PoP warms up. No upfront configuration needed — CDN pulls content on demand. Used by: most web applications (Cloudflare, CloudFront default behavior). PUSH CDN: Origin proactively pushes content to CDN PoPs. Content is available on first request. More work upfront but zero cache misses. Used by: large media companies (Netflix pre-positions movies on CDN PoPs before release).

key_concepts.definition: Controlled by Cache-Control header from origin: max-age=31536000 (cache for 1 year — use for versioned static assets like app.a3f8b2.js), no-cache (always validate with origin before serving — use for frequently changing content), no-store (never cache — use for sensitive data), s-maxage (CDN-specific TTL, overrides max-age), stale-while-revalidate (serve stale content while fetching fresh in background — eliminates latency spikes). EDGE CASE: What if you deploy a bug in a cached JS file? Use cache busting: embed a content hash in the filename (app.[hash].js). New deploy = new hash = new URL = CDN fetches new version. Old version eventually expires.

Modern CDNs can cache dynamic API responses at the edge. Cloudflare Workers run JavaScript at the edge to serve personalized content without hitting origin. Edge computing: run logic at CDN PoPs. AWS CloudFront Functions / Lambda@Edge. Use for: A/B testing (decide variant at edge), geo-based routing, header manipulation, basic auth.

configurable_params.name: TTL per content type
configurable_params.effect: Static assets (images, CSS, JS): 1 year with content hash. API responses: 60-300 seconds. HTML pages: 5-60 minutes.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Longer TTL = higher hit rate but more staleness. Shorter TTL = fresher content but more origin load.

configurable_params.name: Cache key
configurable_params.effect: What uniquely identifies a cached response. Can include: URL + query params + headers (Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language).
configurable_params.tradeoff: More specific cache key = lower hit rate but more correct behavior. Too broad = serving wrong language/encoding to users.
